strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful practical bottleneck: replacing per-image optimization with a trained perturbation generator. Table 2 reports 0.07 seconds per image versus 911.6 seconds for PhotoGuard-D, with lower inference memory usage.

Results provide evidence of a useful protection–quality trade-off on the evaluated inpainting model. On unseen images, DiffVax improves CLIP-T, PSNR, FSIM, and perturbation SSIM over PhotoGuard-D, although editing SSIM is slightly worse.

The evaluation includes held-out images and prompts, loss ablations, JPEG and denoising experiments, and a 67-participant study favoring DiffVax. These provide complementary evidence beyond selected qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The threat model is substantially narrower than the protection claims. The main experiments perturb the foreground while editing its complementary background, using the same segmentation structure. They do not establish protection when an adversary changes the mask or directly inpaints the protected region, potentially removing the perturbation from the conditioning input. This is especially consequential given the motivation around malicious human-image manipulation.

Claims of universal or model-agnostic protection exceed the evidence. The limitations explicitly acknowledge separate training for each editing tool. InstructPix2Pix receives qualitative examples but no quantitative comparison or sufficient training details; cross-model transfer is not demonstrated.

Technical novelty is limited relative to the breadth of the claims: the approach combines an established adversarial perturbation generator, UNet++, an L1 perturbation penalty, and a constant-output editing objective. Comparisons against a learned universal perturbation or alternative amortized attack objectives are missing, and DAYN is discussed extensively without a quantitative comparison.

The quantitative evaluation contains only 75 unseen images from one human-centric dataset, with no reported uncertainty or repeated-run analysis. Image differences from a clean edit do not necessarily establish unsuccessful malicious editing, and matched diffusion randomness is not specified. CLIP-T and human rankings help, but neither supplies a calibrated protection success rate. Whole-image SSIM can also dilute visible perturbations concentrated within the foreground, and the method does not enforce the explicit perturbation budget introduced in Equation 1.

Robustness is tested with one insufficiently specified denoiser and unspecified JPEG settings. There are no compression-quality sweeps, resize/crop tests, or adaptive removal experiments. The evidence supports resilience under the tested configurations, rather than the broad assertion that counter-attack vulnerabilities have been overcome.

The video contribution consists of independently processing frames from four videos and editing them with an image inpainting model. It does not evaluate an actual temporal video editor, temporal consistency, or video compression. Runtime reporting also needs reconciliation: Table 3 gives 0.739 seconds for all 256 frames, whereas Table 2 reports 0.07 seconds per image. Batching, resolution, and timing boundaries are not explained sufficiently to validate the headline speedup.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful optimizer and epoch details. Important omissions include image resolution, diffusion sampling and gradient-backpropagation settings, baseline optimization budgets, precise counter-attack configurations, and whether segmentation is included in runtime. The manuscript references a project webpage and code, but the provided document does not supply an identifiable link.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful scalability problem: replacing per-image adversarial optimization with a trained perturbation generator could make image protection substantially more practical.

Table 2 provides encouraging evidence within the evaluated setting. On unseen images, DiffVax improves CLIP-T from 29.27 to 26.74 and perturbation SSIM from 0.979 to 0.989 relative to PhotoGuard-D, while reporting substantially lower inference time and memory usage.

The evaluation includes qualitative comparisons, a 67-participant human study, loss-component ablations, and a loss-weight sensitivity study. These provide useful supporting evidence beyond a single automatic metric.

The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that separate training is required for each editing tool, and the supplementary InstructPix2Pix examples demonstrate some applicability beyond background inpainting.
weaknesses: The evaluated threat model is substantially narrower than the claimed protection against malicious editing. Perturbations are applied inside the foreground mask, while the main experiments edit its complement using background prompts. This does not establish protection when an attacker changes the mask or edits the protected person directly, potentially removing perturbed pixels from the conditioning input. Such cases are particularly relevant to the motivating misuse scenarios.

The technical novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. The method combines an existing UNet++ perturbation generator with an L1 distortion penalty and an output-to-zero objective, building explicitly on learned adversarial generators. Comparisons against a learned universal perturbation and alternative generator-training objectives are needed to establish what the proposed formulation contributes beyond amortizing adversarial optimization. The prominently discussed DAYN method is also absent from the quantitative evaluation.

Robustness is insufficiently established. Table 5 tests JPEG compression and one denoiser without specifying JPEG quality or the exact denoising model and settings. There are no strength sweeps, adaptive countermeasures, resizing/cropping tests, or quantitative cross-editor transfer experiments. These results support resistance to the tested transformations, not the broad claims of robust or universal protection.

The evaluation is small and only partly held out: the main test contains 75 unseen images and 75 training-seen tuples from a single human-image dataset. No confidence intervals or variability across training runs and editing seeds are reported. Image-distance metrics measure divergence from a reference edit rather than directly establishing failed malicious editing; CLIP-T and the human study help, but neither supplies a calibrated protection success rate.

The video contribution is overstated. The experiment uses four 64-frame videos and applies an image inpainting model independently to each frame. It does not evaluate an actual temporally conditioned video editor, temporal consistency of the perturbations, or video compression. This demonstrates framewise applicability rather than convincing protection against video editing.

The headline speedup is not reconciled with the reported measurements. Table 2 gives 911.6/0.07, approximately 13,000×, whereas Table 3 gives 64 hours/0.739 seconds, approximately 312,000×; neither directly explains the advertised 250,000×. Processing all 256 video frames in 0.739 seconds also requires an explanation relative to the 0.07-second single-image timing. Batching, resolution, timing boundaries, SAM overhead, and amortization of the 22-hour training cost should be documented.

Imperceptibility and baseline fairness need stronger controls. Equation 1 introduces a perturbation budget, but the actual method uses a soft average L1 penalty without a specified hard bound. Whole-image SSIM can conceal visible changes concentrated within the foreground mask. Baseline perturbation budgets and optimization settings are not sufficiently documented, and matched-distortion comparisons or perceptual detection tests are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important details such as image resolution, diffusion sampling steps, scheduler, gradient propagation through sampling, and the exact UNet++ configuration are unspecified. The supplied manuscript also leaves the project-webpage field blank despite claiming code availability. Together with the evaluation gaps, this prevents the otherwise promising efficiency result from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: amortizing image immunization with a learned perturbation generator removes expensive per-image optimization at inference.

Table 2 provides promising evidence of efficiency and effectiveness: 0.07 seconds per image versus 911.6 seconds for PhotoGuard-D, with improved unseen-image PSNR, FSIM, CLIP-T, and perturbation SSIM.
The qualitative examples and 67-participant study support greater visible editing disruption than the tested baselines.
Includes loss-component and loss-weight ablations, held-out images and prompts, and initial experiments with JPEG compression, denoising, and another editing tool.
weaknesses: The demonstrated threat model is substantially narrower than the protection claims. The main experiments perturb a preserved foreground while editing its background. They do not establish protection when an adversary changes the mask or edits the protected subject itself. The limitations section also acknowledges separate training for each editing tool, so the additional InstructPix2Pix examples do not establish cross-model transfer.

Robustness evaluation is insufficient for the broad claims. JPEG quality and the exact denoising configuration are unspecified, and there are no strength sweeps, adaptive countermeasures, or systematic tests of resizing, cropping, and alternative editing configurations. Success against two fixed preprocessing operations does not establish robust prevention.

The comparison omits DAYN, despite positioning it as a principal competing method. Baseline optimization settings and perturbation budgets are insufficiently documented, and matched-distortion comparisons are absent. These omissions make the claimed superiority difficult to assess.

The quantitative generalization evaluation uses only 75 unseen images from the same source dataset, without confidence intervals or repeated-run variability. Image differences and CLIP similarity are useful proxies but do not directly measure whether an intended malicious edit succeeds. The human study measures unrealisticness rather than protection success.

The video contribution is preliminary: four videos are processed and edited frame by frame using an image model. No temporally aware video editor, temporal consistency metric, or video compression evaluation is included, so this mainly demonstrates image-level processing on video frames.

The headline efficiency claim needs reconciliation with the reported measurements. Table 2 implies approximately 13,000× acceleration over PhotoGuard-D, while the much larger video speedup uses a throughput figure whose batching and timing protocol are unexplained. Segmentation overhead and the 22-hour training cost also need clear accounting. Reproducibility is further limited by missing diffusion sampling/backpropagation details and the blank project-webpage field.

The technical novelty is modest relative to learned adversarial perturbation generators already discussed in the paper: the method combines UNet++ with perturbation and output-to-zero losses. This could still yield a valuable practical contribution, but the current comparisons and evaluation do not sufficiently establish the breadth and reliability needed for acceptance.
